title: Caritas in Veritate (2009)
hook: Benedict XVI: charity in truth, and the place of gift in the economy

segments.voice: Yesterday, the death penalty, and the Catechism's revised word for it. Your line was inadmissible. Did you hold a prisoner in mind, even for a moment? Day one thousand three hundred twelve.

What does a paid-for coffee cost? Most mornings at the counter, everyone ends up square: you pay, they hand you the cup, nobody owes anybody. That's a contract, and it's a fine thing. But some mornings the person ahead of you pays for yours and walks out before you can say anything. Nothing was owed. Nothing can be paid back. Pope Benedict the Sixteenth wrote a letter about the economy, about trade and work and development, and right in the middle of the talk of markets he made room for that second kind of moment. Today is that letter, and its claim that gift belongs inside the economy, not only outside it.
screen: `A CONTRACT: EVERYONE'S SQUARE.` → `A STRANGER PAYS FOR YOUR COFFEE.` → `GIFT INSIDE THE ECONOMY.`

segments.voice: First, the title. Caritas in veritate is Latin for charity in truth. Caritas is the old Church word for the love that gives itself, the word behind the Douay-Rheims line in the first letter of John: "God is charity." Benedict pairs it with truth on purpose. Love without truth, he warns, slides into sentiment, a warm feeling that can be bent to mean anything. Truth without love turns cold. He wants them held together, the way Paul writes to the Ephesians: "doing the truth in charity." Second, the economy. Benedict describes more than one way people deal with each other. There's the market, where things are exchanged at an agreed price. There's the state, which shares things out by law. Both, he says, are needed. But neither is enough by itself. Third, the gift. Here's the surprising move. Benedict argues that gratuitousness, giving with no return expected, shouldn't be pushed to the edges, to the charity drive after the real work is done. It should have room within ordinary economic life: in how a business is run, how workers are treated, how a deal is struck. He names this the logic of gift, and he roots it in being human: we didn't make ourselves. We received our lives. Fourth, ordinary life. A shift manager who covers for a worker with a sick child. A landlord who doesn't raise the rent on the old tenant. A shop that keeps a pay-it-forward board. None of these break the market. They just let something into it that a price can't measure. Jesus says it plainly when he sends out his disciples: "Freely have you received, freely give."
screen: `CHARITY IN TRUTH: HELD TOGETHER.` · `THE MARKET AND THE STATE: NEEDED.` · `GIFT BELONGS INSIDE, NOT AT THE EDGE.` · `WHAT A PRICE CAN'T MEASURE.` · then, large: `FREELY HAVE YOU RECEIVED, FREELY GIVE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one gift with no return. Settle, and breathe. Let your mind walk through the next day: the people you'll pay, the people who'll serve you, the people you work beside. Pick one moment where you could give something nobody is owed. Time, a better tip, a covered shift, a word of thanks with a name in it. Choose one where you won't be thanked, or won't be there to see it. Hold it. If you pray, you can offer it to God. If you don't, simply hold the choice quietly. The bell holds the time.
Caritas in Veritate. Charity in truth: Benedict the Sixteenth's letter on the economy, which makes room for gift alongside contract and law. Today's word.
Your line: the logic of gift. Today, in one ordinary transaction, give a little more than the deal requires, and don't mention it. Day one thousand three hundred twelve.

howItsDone: Catholics study Caritas in Veritate in parish and university courses on social teaching, and some Catholic business owners point to its logic of gift when shaping how they treat workers and customers.

fork.setup: you run a small business. a worker's child is sick, and the contract says unpaid leave. what does Benedict's letter push you toward?
options: follow the contract exactly; that's fair.
close the business; markets are the problem.
keep the contract, and let some gift into it.
fork.reveal: Benedict doesn't throw out contracts or markets. he asks that the logic of gift find room inside them, in how people are actually treated.

original.note: Latin: charity in truth, the opening words that give the letter its name.

trapdoor: what you thought: a papal letter telling people to give to charity.
what it means: a letter on the economy saying love must be held with truth, and that gift belongs inside economic life, not only at its edges.
what a scholar hears: an echo of Ephesians 4:15, veritas in caritate, turned around, and a case for gratuitousness alongside contract and law.

sources.ref: Caritas in Veritate, introduction and chapter 3 (charity and truth; market, state and the logic of gift; gratuitousness)

notes: Paraphrases of Caritas in Veritate (charity without truth becomes sentimentality; market and state both needed but insufficient; the principle of gratuitousness and the logic of gift within normal economic activity; gift experienced because we did not make ourselves) should be checked against the text, especially sections 2–3 and 34–39.
Trapdoor floor 3 says the title turns Ephesians 4:15 around (veritas in caritate); confirm the Vulgate wording and that the encyclical itself draws this link.
The coffee-shop and workplace examples are illustrations, not from the encyclical.
Year (2009) kept out of the spoken text under the claims rule; it stays in the index title.

Editor pass: reworked the hook (a counter scene echoed day 1308; dropped 'to the whole Church', since the letter is also addressed to all people of good will, and the claim that Benedict 'put that scene' in the letter); Benedict XVI spoken as 'Benedict the Sixteenth'; softened the paraphrase of why gift is human; 'the Tuesday' renamed to avoid repeating day 1321's image.
